title: Predicting What Comes Next: Sequences and Progressions

sections.title: Sum of the First n Natural Numbers

slides.title: Patterns All Around Us
slides.kicker: Nature, music, finance: patterns are everywhere!
bullets: Patterns in nature, art, music and finance help us make sense of the world and predict what comes next.
In mathematics, a sequence is a special kind of pattern formed by numbers or other objects arranged in a particular order.
Understanding sequences shows how numbers grow, shrink or repeat, and helps us solve real-life problems.
slides.note: Spot the pattern, predict the future.

slides.title: Sequences You Already Know
slides.kicker: Old friends from Grades 6, 7 and 8 return.
bullets: Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, ... where every term is one more than the previous term.
Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, ... with a difference of 2 between any two consecutive terms.
Triangular numbers: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, ... and square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, ...
The three dots mean the sequence continues indefinitely.
slides.note: You have met all four before.

slides.title: Terms, Finite, Infinite
slides.kicker: Every number in the line is a term.
bullets: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers where each number is a term of the sequence.
In the square numbers, 1 is the first term, 4 is the second term and 25 is the fifth term.
The four famous sequences are infinite, but 6, 12, 24, 48, 96 is a finite sequence of five terms.

right.title: Infinite
items: The dots mean it goes on forever

slides.note: Can you spot a finite sequence in your day?

slides.title: Triangular Number Secret
slides.kicker: Each triangular number hides a running sum.
bullets: Rewrite the triangular numbers as sums: 1 = 1, 3 = 1 + 2, 6 = 1 + 2 + 3, 10 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.
Each term is the sum of the natural numbers up to that term; 15, the fifth triangular number, equals 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.
Among the first six terms, the differences between consecutive triangular numbers are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
slides.note: Stack dots in a triangle and see.

slides.title: Name Any Term: tn
slides.kicker: Position n goes in, term value comes out.
bullets: We use notation like tn, sn or un for the term in the nth position of a sequence.
An explicit formula uses the term's position number, n, to calculate its value.
With an explicit rule you can find the 20th, 53rd or 300th term directly, without knowing any previous term.
slides.note: Formula mila, term mila.

slides.title: The Odd Numbers Formula
slides.kicker: un = 2n - 1 builds every odd number.
bullets: The explicit rule un = 2n - 1 gives the nth term of the odd number sequence.
Each substitution lands exactly on the next odd number, so the rule truly captures the sequence.
slides.note: One rule, infinite odd numbers.

slides.title: Is It a Term?
slides.kicker: Solve un = k and check that n is natural.
bullets: An explicit rule can test whether a number belongs to a sequence and find its position.
For 137 in the odd numbers: solving 2n - 1 = 137 gives n = 69, so 137 is the 69th term.
For sn = 5n - 2, solving 5n - 2 = 471 gives n = 94.6, not a natural number, so 471 is not a term.
n must be a natural number because positions in a sequence are 1, 2, 3, ...
slides.note: No natural n, no seat in the sequence.

slides.title: Any Term, Instantly
slides.kicker: Reach term 1000 in one step.
bullets: Example 2 uses sn = 5n - 2, whose first six terms are 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28.
The 100th term is 5 × 100 - 2 = 498 and the 1000th term is 5 × 1000 - 2 = 4998.
One substitution beats writing out a thousand terms; that is the power of an explicit rule.
slides.note: 1000th term? Bas ek second.

slides.title: Rule From Previous Terms
slides.kicker: A recursive rule grows each term from the last.
bullets: A recursive rule describes a sequence by relating terms to previous terms.
For 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, ... each term is 3 more than the one before: t(n) = t(n-1) + 3 for n >= 2.
Write the whole rule as t1 = 1, t(n) = t(n-1) + 3 with n taking values 2, 3, 4, ...
You must know the earlier terms before the rule can produce the next ones.
slides.note: Domino effect: one term pushes the next.

slides.title: Climbing a Recursive Ladder
slides.kicker: Feed each term back into the formula.
bullets: Example 3: u1 = 1 and u(n) = 2u(n-1) + 3 for n >= 2.
The first four terms are 1, 5, 13, 29; keep computing later terms to test whether 133 ever appears.
slides.note: Double, add 3, repeat.

slides.title: A Wilder Recursion
slides.kicker: Multiply the previous term by one less.
bullets: Example 4: s1 = 3 and s(n) = s(n-1) × (s(n-1) - 1) for n >= 2.
The first four terms are 3, 6, 30, 870; recursive rules can grow surprisingly fast.
slides.note: 3, 6, 30, 870: hold on tight!

slides.title: Virahanka-Fibonacci Magic
slides.kicker: Add the previous two terms and watch it grow.
bullets: A recursive rule does not only involve the previous term; it could involve the previous two or more terms.
The famous Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence starts V1 = 1, V2 = 2, with V(n) = V(n-1) + V(n-2) for n >= 3.
Each term is obtained by adding the previous two; the next two terms are 55 and 89.
slides.note: You met this one in earlier grades!

slides.title: Squares Grow Stage by Stage
slides.kicker: Four new squares join at every stage.
bullets: A growing pattern of squares counts 1, 5, 9, 13 tiny squares in its first four stages.
At each stage, 4 squares get added to the corners of the pattern in the earlier stage.
slides.note: A straight line climbing up: that is a clue.

slides.title: Build the Rule: 4n - 3
slides.kicker: First term plus n minus 1 jumps of 4.
bullets: From t1 = 1, t2 = 1 + 1 × 4, t3 = 1 + 2 × 4, the nth term is t(n) = 1 + (n - 1) × 4, which simplifies to t(n) = 4n - 3.
The first six terms are 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, so Stage 5 has 17 squares and Stage 6 has 21.
In this rule, 1 is the first term of the sequence and 4 is the common difference.
slides.note: Stage 20? 77 squares, no counting needed.

slides.title: What Makes an AP
slides.kicker: Same difference between every neighbouring pair.
bullets: Sequences in which the difference between consecutive terms is constant are known as arithmetic progressions, or APs.
In general an AP is a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, ..., a + (n - 1) × d, where a is the first term and d is the common difference.
For 1, 4, 7, 10, ... the rule is t(n) = 1 + (n - 1) × 3 with common difference 3.
The sequence 11, 7, 3, -1, -5, ... decreases by 4, so it is also an AP, with first term 11 and common difference -4.
slides.note: d can be negative too.

slides.title: AP or Not AP?
slides.kicker: Test the differences before you decide.
bullets: Natural numbers and odd numbers are APs: their differences are the constant values 1 and 2.
Triangular numbers are not an AP: their differences among the first six terms are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, which keep changing.
The sequence of prime numbers has no clear regularity in its rule, so it is not an AP either.
slides.note: Constant difference is the AP entry ticket.

slides.title: Add 1 to 10 Smartly
slides.kicker: Write it forward, write it back, then add.
bullets: Each corresponding pair, 1 + 10, 2 + 9, 3 + 8 and so on up to 10 + 1, adds up to 11.
Adding the two equations: 2S = 11 added 10 times = 110, so S = 55.
slides.note: Ten pairs of 11: neat trick, na?

slides.title: The Formula for Any n
slides.kicker: Reverse, add, divide by two. Done.
bullets: Let S = 1 + 2 + ... + n; written backwards it is S = n + (n - 1) + ... + 1.
Adding the two expressions gives 2S = n(n + 1), so S = n(n + 1)/2.
Check with n = 10: 10 × 11 / 2 = 55, matching the pairing trick exactly.
slides.note: Sn = n(n+1)/2. Yaad kar lo!

slides.title: See It as a Rectangle
slides.kicker: Two dot triangles make one tidy rectangle.
bullets: Draw two sets of circles for the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6, one above and one below a zigzag partition.
The total number of circles forms a 7 × 6 rectangular array, so 2 × (1 + 2 + ... + 6) = 7 × 6.
In general 2 × (1 + 2 + ... + n) = n × (n + 1), which again gives Sn = n(n + 1)/2.
slides.note: Triangles love to become rectangles.

slides.title: Aryabhata Got There First
slides.kicker: The first written record of this sum formula.
bullets: The first known written mention of the result Sn = n(n + 1)/2 is in Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya, Chapter 2, Verse 19.
That verse provides two ways to calculate the sums.
Use the formula yourself: 1 + 2 + ... + 100 = 100 × 101 / 2 = 5050.
slides.note: A Bhaaratiya classic, first penned by Aryabhata.

slides.title: Doubling Squares Pattern
slides.kicker: Every stage doubles the green squares.
bullets: A growing pattern of squares counts 3, 6, 12, 24 green squares in its first four stages.
At each stage, the number of green squares is doubled, twice the number in the previous stage.
The successive counts are 3, 3 + 3 = 6, 6 + 6 = 12, 12 + 12 = 24, and so on.
slides.note: See the curve swoop up? Different from the AP!

slides.title: Multiply, Don't Add
slides.kicker: Common ratio 2 powers this pattern.
bullets: Rewrite the counts as 3, 3 × 2, 3 × 2^2, 3 × 2^3, ... so the nth term is t(n) = 3 × 2^(n - 1).
As a recursive formula, t1 = 3 and t(n) = 2t(n-1) for n >= 2; the first six terms are 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96.
The constant multiplier is the common ratio: 6/3 = 12/6 = 24/12 = 48/24 = 96/48 = 2.
slides.note: Multiply by 2 and the terms double up.

slides.title: The GP Family Portrait
slides.kicker: a, ar, ar squared, ar cubed and onwards.
bullets: Such a sequence with a common ratio is known as a geometric progression, or GP.
In general a GP is a, ar, ar^2, ar^3, ..., ar^(n - 1), where a is the first term, r is the common ratio and t(n) = ar^(n - 1).
slides.note: r = -1 makes the terms flip sides.

slides.title: AP versus GP
slides.kicker: Adding d versus multiplying by r.
bullets: An AP adds the same difference d each step, like 1, 4, 7, 10, ... with d = 3.
A GP multiplies by the same ratio r each step, like 3, 6, 12, 24, ... with r = 2, so each term is twice the last.
Even fractions can be ratios: 5, 15/4, 45/16, 135/64, ... is a GP with common ratio 3/4.
slides.note: Add d or multiply by r: pick your growth.

flashcards.front: What is a sequence in mathematics?
flashcards.back: An ordered list of numbers where each number is a term of the sequence.

flashcards.front: In the square number sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, ..., which term is 25?
flashcards.back: 25 is the fifth term, since the sequence runs 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.

flashcards.front: Is 6, 12, 24, 48, 96 a finite or infinite sequence?
flashcards.back: It is a finite sequence of exactly five terms; it stops after 96.

flashcards.front: Why are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 called triangular numbers?
flashcards.back: Each term is the sum of natural numbers up to that term, like 15 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.

flashcards.front: What does an explicit formula use to calculate a term?
flashcards.back: It uses the term's position number n to calculate the value of the nth term directly.

flashcards.front: Write the explicit rule for the odd number sequence.
flashcards.back: un = 2n - 1; substituting n = 1, 2, 3 gives 1, 3, 5, ...

flashcards.front: Which term of the odd number sequence is 137?
flashcards.back: The 69th term, because solving 2n - 1 = 137 gives n = 69.

flashcards.front: For sn = 5n - 2, why is 471 not a term?
flashcards.back: Solving 5n - 2 = 471 gives n = 94.6, and n must be a natural number.

flashcards.front: What is a recursive rule for a sequence?
flashcards.back: A rule that describes the sequence by relating terms to previous terms; the earlier terms must be known first.

flashcards.front: Give a recursive rule for 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, ...
flashcards.back: t1 = 1 and t(n) = t(n-1) + 3 for n >= 2; each term is 3 more than the previous one.

flashcards.front: State the Virahanka-Fibonacci rule.
flashcards.back: V1 = 1, V2 = 2, and V(n) = V(n-1) + V(n-2) for n >= 3; add the previous two terms.

flashcards.front: First four terms of u1 = 1, u(n) = 2u(n-1) + 3?
flashcards.back: 1, 5, 13, 29: double the previous term and add 3 each time.

flashcards.front: What makes a sequence an arithmetic progression?
flashcards.back: The difference between consecutive terms is constant; such sequences are called APs.

flashcards.front: Write the general form of an arithmetic progression.
flashcards.back: a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, ..., a + (n - 1) × d, where a is the first term and d the common difference.

flashcards.front: For the AP 11, 7, 3, -1, -5, ..., what are a and d?
flashcards.back: First term a = 11 and common difference d = -4, since the numbers decrease by 4.

flashcards.front: What is the nth term of 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, ...?
flashcards.back: t(n) = 1 + (n - 1) × 4, which simplifies to t(n) = 4n - 3.

flashcards.front: What is Sn, the sum of the first n natural numbers?
flashcards.back: Sn = n(n + 1)/2, found by adding the sum forward and backward.

flashcards.front: Find 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 10 without adding one by one.
flashcards.back: Pair the forward and backward rows: 2S = 11 added 10 times = 110, so S = 55.

flashcards.front: Where does the sum formula first appear in writing?
flashcards.back: In Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya, Chapter 2, Verse 19, the first known written mention.

flashcards.front: What makes a sequence a geometric progression?
flashcards.back: Each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a constant, called the common ratio.

flashcards.front: Write the general form of a GP and its nth term.
flashcards.back: a, ar, ar^2, ar^3, ..., ar^(n - 1), with t(n) = ar^(n - 1); a is the first term, r the common ratio.

flashcards.front: What is the common ratio of 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, ...?
flashcards.back: The ratio is -1: multiplying each term by -1 flips it to the next one.

flashcards.front: Give the nth term of 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, ...
flashcards.back: t(n) = 3 × 2^(n - 1); the first term is 3 and the common ratio is 2.

quiz.q: Which sequence is 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, ...?
quiz.why: Triangular numbers are the sums 1, 1 + 2, 1 + 2 + 3, and so on.

quiz.q: In the sequence of square numbers, which term is 25?
quiz.why: The squares run 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, so 25 is the fifth term.

quiz.q: The list 6, 12, 24, 48, 96 is best described as...
options: A finite sequence of five terms
quiz.why: The book gives it as a finite sequence of five terms, unlike the endless dotted sequences.

quiz.q: Among the first six triangular numbers, the differences between consecutive terms are...
quiz.why: From 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 the gaps are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, so the differences are not constant.

quiz.q: The explicit rule un = 2n - 1 generates which sequence?
quiz.why: Substituting n = 1, 2, 3 gives 1, 3, 5, the odd numbers.

quiz.q: Using un = 2n - 1, what is the 53rd term of the odd number sequence?
quiz.why: u53 = 2 × 53 - 1 = 105, found without any earlier terms.

quiz.q: For sn = 5n - 2, which position does 308 occupy?
quiz.why: Solving 5n - 2 = 308 gives 5n = 310 and n = 62, a natural number.

quiz.q: For sn = 5n - 2, why does the membership check for 471 fail?
options: Solving gives n = 94.6, which is not a natural number
Solving gives n = 94, which is too small
All terms of this sequence are even
quiz.why: 5n - 2 = 471 leads to 5n = 473 and n = 94.6, and positions must be natural numbers.

quiz.q: A recursive rule finds each new term using...
quiz.why: Recursive rules relate each term to previous terms, so earlier terms must be known first.

quiz.q: The rule is u1 = 1 and u(n) = 2u(n-1) + 3 for n >= 2. Its first four terms are...
For s1 = 3 and s(n) = s(n-1) × (s(n-1) - 1), the fourth term is...
The next two terms of the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, ... are...
quiz.why: Each term is the sum of the previous two: 21 + 34 = 55 and 34 + 55 = 89.

quiz.q: In an arithmetic progression, the difference between consecutive terms is...
quiz.why: A constant difference between consecutive terms is exactly what defines an AP.

quiz.q: In the growing square pattern with stages 1, 5, 9, 13, what happens at each new stage?
options: 4 squares are added at the corners
quiz.why: At each stage, 4 squares get added to the corners of the earlier stage's pattern.

quiz.q: The stage counts follow t(n) = 4n - 3. How many squares are in Stage 20?
Which of these sequences is NOT an arithmetic progression?
quiz.why: Triangular numbers have differences 2, 3, 4, 5, which are not constant; the others are APs with d = -4, 3 and 2.

quiz.q: The sum of the first ten natural numbers is...
quiz.why: Pairing forward and backward rows gives 2S = 11 × 10 = 110, so S = 55.

quiz.q: Using Sn = n(n + 1)/2, what is 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 100?
quiz.why: 100 × 101 / 2 = 5050; note that 10100 is the doubled sum 2S.

quiz.q: Pictorially, two copies of the dots for 1 + 2 + ... + 6 together form which array?
quiz.why: The circles above and below the zigzag partition fill a 7 × 6 array, so 2S = 7 × 6.

quiz.q: The first known written mention of Sn = n(n + 1)/2 appears in...
quiz.why: The Aryabhatiya, Chapter 2, Verse 19, carries the first known written mention of this result.

quiz.q: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... is a geometric progression. Its common ratio is...
quiz.why: Each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by 2.

quiz.q: 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, ... is a geometric progression because...
options: Each term is the previous term times -1
The terms are all whole numbers
The difference between terms is constant
quiz.why: Multiplying by the constant ratio -1 produces every term, which is exactly what a GP needs.

quiz.q: For the GP 5, 15/4, 45/16, 135/64, ..., the nth term is...
quiz.why: Each ratio is (15/4) ÷ 5 = 3/4, so with a = 5 the nth term is t(n) = 5 × (3/4)^(n - 1).

quiz.q: What is the key difference between an AP and a GP?
options: An AP multiplies by a constant, a GP adds one
A GP must always grow faster than an AP
An AP adds a constant difference, a GP multiplies by a constant ratio
quiz.why: APs add the common difference d each step; GPs multiply by the common ratio r each step.

examples.title: Any Term of the Odd Numbers, Instantly
examples.problem: The odd number sequence has the explicit rule un = 2n - 1. Find the 53rd term, the 108th term and the 1170th term.
steps: The rule uses only the position n, so substitute each position straight into un = 2n - 1.

examples.title: Testing Two Numbers for Membership
examples.problem: The sequence generated by sn = 5n - 2 begins 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28, ... Check whether 308 and 471 are terms of this sequence.
steps: A number is a term only if solving sn = k gives a natural number n.
For 308: solve 5n - 2 = 308, so 5n = 310 and n = 62, which is a natural number.
So 308 is the 62nd term of the sequence.
For 471: solve 5n - 2 = 471, so 5n = 473 and n = 94.6, which is not a natural number.
Since positions must be 1, 2, 3, ..., 471 cannot be a term.
examples.answer: 308 is the 62nd term of the sequence, and 471 is not a term at all.

examples.title: Climbing the Recursive Ladder
examples.problem: A sequence is given by u1 = 1 and u(n) = 2u(n-1) + 3 for n >= 2. Find the first four terms, and check whether 133 is a term of this sequence.
steps: Start from u1 = 1 and feed each term back into the rule.
The terms jump from 125 to 253 without ever landing on 133.
examples.answer: The first four terms are 1, 5, 13, 29, and 133 is not a term of this sequence.

examples.title: A Geometric Progression in Fractions
examples.problem: Check whether the sequence 5, 15/4, 45/16, 135/64, ... is a geometric progression, and find its nth term.
steps: A GP needs the same ratio between every pair of consecutive terms, so divide each term by the one before it.
Every ratio equals 3/4, so this is a GP with first term a = 5 and common ratio r = 3/4.
Apply the general rule t(n) = ar^(n - 1) = 5 × (3/4)^(n - 1).
examples.answer: Yes, it is a GP with common ratio 3/4 and nth term t(n) = 5 × (3/4)^(n - 1).

steps.label: Spot a Pattern
steps.detail: Patterns in nature, art, music and finance point to number sequences.

steps.label: List the Terms
steps.detail: Write the numbers in order; each one is a term, finite or infinite.

steps.label: Guess the Rule
steps.detail: Ask how terms grow: adding, multiplying, or running sums.

steps.label: Write Explicit Rule
steps.detail: Write the rule using n, like un = 2n - 1, to reach any term at once.

steps.label: Write Recursive Rule
steps.detail: Relate each term to previous ones, like t(n) = t(n-1) + 3, starting from t1.

steps.label: Check Any Position
steps.detail: Solve t(n) = k for n; the answer must be a natural number.

steps.label: Name the Progression
steps.detail: Constant difference means an AP; constant ratio means a GP.

steps.label: Predict and Sum
steps.detail: Use t(n) and Sn = n(n + 1)/2 to predict terms and totals, like Aryabhata did.
